questions.q: Why does a slow AI inference request break the normal 'just add instances' scaling plan, per this lesson?
options: AI requests cannot be load balanced at all
Holding an open connection for every concurrent slow request can exhaust connections, timeouts, or GPU capacity before autoscaling catches up
AI requests are always rejected by default
Instances cannot process more than one request per day
questions.explain: A request that takes seconds to tens of seconds, held open synchronously for every concurrent caller, strains resources faster than autoscaling (which itself is slow for GPU instances) can respond.

questions.q: In the asynchronous pattern described in this lesson, what does the client receive immediately after submitting a request?
options: The final generated response
A job ID, with the result fetched or pushed later
A permanent error message
A new container image
questions.explain: Async returns a job ID right away; the client polls or receives a webhook for the actual result once a worker finishes it.

questions.q: What does a queue in front of autoscaling buy you that autoscaling alone doesn't, according to this lesson?
options: It eliminates the need for autoscaling entirely
It guarantees zero cost regardless of traffic
It makes GPU instances start instantly
Requests can wait briefly while instances catch up, so a burst is delayed rather than rejected
questions.explain: The queue turns 'need more capacity right now' into 'capacity can catch up shortly' -- nothing gets rejected outright.

questions.q: What happens to a job that keeps failing after several retry attempts, per this lesson's queueing pattern?
options: It's silently discarded with no record
It's automatically resubmitted forever until it succeeds
It's moved to a dead-letter queue and set aside, so it stops blocking the rest of the queue
It's immediately escalated to a human on every single failure
questions.explain: A dead-letter queue is exactly where repeatedly-failing jobs land, keeping a poison-pill request from consuming worker time indefinitely.

questions.q: Without a dead-letter queue, what risk does this lesson say a single malformed or impossible request poses?
options: It could consume retry attempts and worker capacity that healthy jobs need
It would automatically crash the entire container registry
It would permanently disable autoscaling for the whole service
It would corrupt the model's weights in GPU memory
questions.explain: Without a DLQ, a poison-pill job can block or endlessly retry, starving healthy jobs of worker time.
